note: Hebrew ketonet passim probably means a robe reaching to the palms and soles (pas = extremity), i.e. a long-sleeved, full-length garment; "many colours" follows the Septuagint's poikilos and is a guess. Also in vv. 23 and 32. Context: a long robe with sleeves (medium confidence). The only other use (2 Sam 13:18-19) is the robe of the king's virgin daughters: a garment of status, described by its cut, not its colours.
Hebrew nekot and lot are aromatic gums (tragacanth and labdanum/ladanum); lot is not myrrh, which is mor in Hebrew.

kjv: go down into the grave unto my son
mine: go down to my son in Sheol
note: Hebrew she'olah is Sheol, the underworld abode of the dead; the KJV alternates between "grave", "hell" and "pit", which obscures that it is one consistent term.
The Masoretic text reads hammedanim (Medanites, cf. Medan in Gen 25:2); the KJV follows the Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint and Vulgate, which harmonise with "Midianites" in v. 28.
